stem:
A 9-month-old boy has had profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days. He is drowsy, with mottled, cold hands and feet, deep sighing breathing, and deeply sunken eyes and fontanelle.

| Measurement | Value | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weight | 8 kg | — |
| Capillary refill time | 5 seconds | — |
| Heart rate | 190/min | — |
| Sodium | 137 mmol/L | 135-145 |
| Potassium | 3.8 mmol/L | 3.5-5.0 |
| Bicarbonate | 12 mmol/L | 18-25 |
| Urea | 11.8 mmol/L | 1.8-6.4 |
| Glucose | 4.4 mmol/L | 3.6-5.4 |

An intravenous cannula is in place. Which fluid should he receive first?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral rehydration solution via NG tube
options.explanation: Enteral rehydration suits mild to moderate dehydration. He is shocked, with poor perfusion and a reduced conscious state, so IV resuscitation comes first.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Hypotonic saline is not recommended for routine use in children because of the risk of hyponatraemia, and a slow infusion does not treat shock.

options.label: C
options.explanation: This is RCH's standard fluid for maintenance and deficit replacement once perfusion is restored. It is not the first fluid in shock.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Correct. He has severe dehydration with shock: drowsy, mottled, CRT 5 s and acidotic. Give 10-20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride as fast as possible, then reassess.

options.label: E
options.explanation: A glucose-only bolus becomes free water once the glucose is used, so it does not restore circulating volume and risks hyponatraemia. His glucose is normal.

context: Shock from gastroenteritis needs a 10-20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride and reassessment. Oral or NG rehydration is for mild to moderate dehydration without shock.
